Run 2-hour canary with 512-token median on dedicated pool (Priya to schedule)

action_items: Priya Shah: prepare canary run template and schedule (due: 2026-02-24)
Ethan Miller: send pricing delta for dedicated vs hosted for expected qps (due: 2026-02-23)

summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest lab benchmarks vs customer's incumbent baseline. Observed lower median latency on Redwood hosted but slightly higher p95 under bursty tails; throughput aligns when using continuous batching and KV caching. Discussed tuning: reduce batch timeout, enable prefix caching for conversational flows, and try int8 quantization on dedicated pool. Agreed next steps: schedule canary run with 2-hour steady-state traffic, exchange security docs, and Redwood to provide pricing delta.
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Miller: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick roll call?
[00:07] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Lena here. Marcus here. Sofia, Tom also on.
[00:12] Ethan Miller: Great, Ethan from Redwood, Priya our SE and Carlos from customer success. quick agenda - review the numbers you sent yesterday, triage the tail latency, and agree canary timing.
[00:27] Priya Shah: I pulled the lab runs this morning, um the median token latency on our hosted endpoint was 22 ms per token at the 128 context profile, the incumbent baseline you shared was about 35 ms median. so median is a win for us.
[00:41] Marcus Liu: Yeah that's promising. but our concern is the p95 during burst loads - we saw p95s spike above 800 ms with the baseline, and in your run p95 was about 620 ms, still better but not as stable.
[00:56] Priya Shah: Right so the p95 gap is smaller than median, we think that's mostly queueing at the batching layer when you have sudden query fan-out. you have shorter sequences normally but occasional long docs, is that right?
[01:12] Tom Bennett: correct, we have a long-tail; maybe 5% of requests hit 1k+ tokens with attachments; that's what causes jitter.
[01:21] Priya Shah: ok that matches. two levers we recommended: 1) lower batch hold timeout for low-latency routes, 2) enable prefix/KV cache for your chat flows to avoid re-computing.
[01:34] Dr. Lena Ortiz: can you explain prefix/KV cache a bit more? sometimes our team confuses kv cache with regular caching.
[01:40] Priya Shah: yeah simplified: KV cache stores the model's key/value state for autoregressive generation so repeated prefixes don't re-run the same compute. for conversational flows it's often a 30-60% token compute savings. it's different from response caching which is whole-response.
[01:55] Marcus Liu: got it. in our infra we use CloudEnd for embeddings and they have a different cache strategy. any compatibility issues moving cache to dedicated?
[02:05] Priya Shah: no compatibility issues. on dedicated the cache is co-located on the GPU node and we can persist warm caches across warm pools if you pin sessions. small caveat: if you evict nodes at scale you need to handle cache cold-starts.
[02:18] Ethan Miller: also worth noting the runtime can do continuous batching which reduces cost but can add a bit of variance on the tail. for strict SLOs we recommend a mix: low-latency route with a small batch and a background route that batches aggressively for lower cost.
[02:34] Sofia Reyes: curious about quantization — you mentioned int8 earlier in the doc. does that impact p95?
[02:40] Priya Shah: int8 reduces compute by ~1.8-2x on our tests. median improves a lot, p95 sometimes improves but can be unpredictable if your workloads are very bursty and memory-bound. on dedicated it's a safer bet because you control node sizing.
[02:56] Dr. Lena Ortiz: the security team will want to see KMS and SOC2 details before any dedicated talk.
[03:02] Carlos Vega: yes, Carlos will share the SOC2 report and KMS integration guide after the call.
[03:07] Ethan Miller: note for the day-to-day, the most immediate wins we've already shipped in your POC: continuous batch tuning and 2x cache hits on repeated prompts. the lab runs you received yesterday used synthetic traffic mirroring your provided distribution but we changed the tail to stress the system.
[03:23] Marcus Liu: we saw that. question: the synthetic traffic showed higher throughput than our real production because we removed some auth layers; how should we interpret the throughput numbers?
[03:32] Priya Shah: good call — synthetic bench often removes perimeter latency. our recommendation is to run a short canary in your VPC (on dedicated or private) to measure real e2e numbers. that will also include your auth, LB, and any ingress latency.
[03:46] Tom Bennett: do you have a template for the canary? we prefer reproducible steps.
[03:50] Priya Shah: yes we'll share a canary runbook with the exact traffic profile, expected p50/p95 thresholds, and alerting hooks.
[03:57] Ethan Miller: quick dive into the numbers: yesterday's bench — steady-state qps 220 with 256 token median, throughput matched baseline when using a 2x batch size and enable prefix cache. p95 improved by ~18% versus baseline in that steady phase.
[04:14] Dr. Lena Ortiz: that's the sweet spot then. but again tails during spikes are still a worry. any immediate config changes?
[04:21] Priya Shah: two immediate config changes to try: reduce batch hold time from 10 ms to 4 ms on your low-latency route; second, enable per-route KV caching TTL of 10 minutes for active sessions.
[04:33] Marcus Liu: what's the operational cost of lowering hold time? more cost, less efficiency?
[04:38] Priya Shah: slightly higher cost because you reduce batching efficiency. but we can quantify — Ethan will send a pricing delta showing expected cost at your qps distribution.
[04:46] Ethan Miller: yeah I'll run the numbers for dedicated vs hosted assuming the same traffic profile and show cost per 1M tokens and an estimate for what's needed to keep p95 under 500 ms.
[04:56] Sofia Reyes: and if we go dedicated, how fast to scale up? our traffic is spiky, we don't want wasted reserved capacity.
[05:02] Priya Shah: Dedicated supports burst policies — you can keep a smaller reserved pool and allow bursts to scale into a buffer. there's also auto-scaling for queued requests. for quick spikes we recommend a small steady pool plus autoscale.
[05:14] Tom Bennett: any fallout for rate limiting or quotas when scaling? we have downstream rate limits on some third-party connectors.
[05:19] Priya Shah: we integrate with your existing rate limiters, but as part of canary we'll provide a config that maps your inbound keys to routes to avoid hitting third-party limits.
[05:28] Marcus Liu: from a security perspective, can you confirm data retention during dedicated runs? we need to ensure no logs leave our VPC.
[05:34] Carlos Vega: we have a Private option that keeps everything in your VPC and audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM. the standard dedicated also supports KMS, HSM integrations, and retains logs per your retention policy. I'll link the security packet.
[05:47] Dr. Lena Ortiz: on the subject of metrics: can you expose token-level latency and per-model memory pressure so our SREs can set alerts?
[05:55] Priya Shah: yes we can stream token-level histograms to your datadog or prometheus, and surface model-level GPU memory metrics.
[06:03] Ethan Miller: ok jumping back to the p95 triage — if after the canary p95 still spikes, next step would be: 1) run a focused tail-run with long sequences and enable kv pinning, 2) consider moving those long-running requests to a separate heavy-model tier, or 3) use smaller context windows for summarization.
[06:20] Marcus Liu: do you have an example of the heavy-model tier config?
[06:24] Priya Shah: yes: dedicated nodes sized with 48GB plus a 1.2x concurrency cap, and you set the routing policy to route >800 token requests to that tier. it'll cost more per request but keeps the low-latency path clean.
[06:38] Tom Bennett: for the canary, what duration do you recommend?
[06:41] Priya Shah: minimum 2 hours steady-state plus a 30-minute stress window. that'll give a reasonable p95 estimate and catch warm/cold starts.
[06:50] Dr. Lena Ortiz: ok let's schedule that for this week.
[06:53] Ethan Miller: action items we'll put in the notes. also quick question: you mentioned your incumbent... was that ApexAI?
[06:59] Sofia Reyes: yes most of our production is on ApexAI and a small part on CloudEnd.
[07:04] Ethan Miller: thanks. one note about our benchmarks — there might be transcription mismatches in the report; we saw a few model names escaped as 'red wood' in the logs; that was just OCR oddness.
[07:15] Marcus Liu: haha ok good to know.
[07:18] Priya Shah: final technical note: if you plan to test int8 quantize we recommend running a regression eval on your prompt set because small numeric diffs can surface on corner cases.
[07:29] Dr. Lena Ortiz: we'll run that. also can you confirm SSO/SAML integration timeline? security wants that before production.
[07:36] Carlos Vega: SSO is standard; we have a one-day setup for SAML with your IdP and a smoke test. I'll coordinate with Tom.
[07:44] Tom Bennett: perfect.
[07:46] Ethan Miller: ok closing with a quick recap and owners. Priya will run canary template and lead the run. Ethan will send pricing and cost delta. Carlos will share SOC2 and KMS docs. Tom will provide traffic distribution. we aiming to have canary by 2026-02-24.
[08:05] Dr. Lena Ortiz: sounds good. any final quick questions?
[08:09] Marcus Liu: none from me.
[08:11] Sofia Reyes: no. thanks everyone.
[08:14] Ethan Miller: thanks all, talk soon.
[08:17] -- End of recording --
